summary.brief: A DIY tutorial shows how to make a faux beaded curtain by gluing colored paper circles onto black yarn strands and hanging them in front of a window.
summary.detailed: The video begins with the presenter laying out supplies—black yarn, a 1‑inch circle punch, scissors, a hot‑glue gun, glue sticks, and assorted paint‑chip circles in Halloween and autumn colors. She punches or cuts the circles, measures the window and cuts yarn to length, then folds the top end of each strand over and ties a simple knot to form a hanging loop. Working from the top down, she applies a dab of hot glue to a paint‑chip circle, places the yarn between two circles, and presses them together before the glue sets; she repeats this, adding four to six circles at a time, mixing colors randomly to avoid patterns. After the glue dries, each completed strand—some entirely painted, others plain yarn alternating—is ready. The strands are then hung side‑by‑side in front of the window, where daylight and later evening light illuminate the colorful “beads.” The presenter thanks viewers, invites them to try the project, and the video ends with the usual end‑screen and channel‑promotion graphics.

action.detailed: Apply hot glue to each colored paper circle, sandwich the black yarn between circles, press them together, repeat to build multiple strands, tie a loop at the top of each strand, and hang the finished strands together as a decorative curtain.

summary.brief: A DIY tutorial shows how to make a beaded‑style curtain by punching paper circles, gluing them onto black yarn, and hanging the finished strands.
summary.detailed: The video opens with a title screen of red lipstick lips and the text “The Easy DIY”. It then shows a window already decorated with colorful beaded‑style curtains. A list of supplies appears: black yarn, a 1‑inch circle punch, scissors, a hot‑glue gun with sticks, and paint‑chip swatches. The creator’s hands punch circular pieces from colored paper or cardboard and collect them in a bowl. The yarn is measured to the window width, cut to length, and a loop is tied at one end. Hot glue is applied to the yarn and each punched circle—sometimes sandwiched between two paint‑chip pieces—is pressed onto the glue before it sets, with colors mixed randomly to avoid a pattern. Several circles are attached at a time while the glue dries, and the process is repeated to build multiple strands; the final set includes seventeen strands with painted circles and sixteen strands of plain yarn. These strands are hung across the window as a decorative curtain. The video concludes with the strands laid out on the floor, a small doll placed among the circles, and a brief look at a candy‑corn garland in the background.

summary_sent_to_llm.root_summary: The video begins with the presenter laying out supplies—black yarn, a 1‑inch circle punch, scissors, a hot‑glue gun, glue sticks, and assorted paint‑chip circles in Halloween and autumn colors. She punches or cuts the circles, measures the window and cuts yarn to length, then folds the top end of each strand over and ties a simple knot to form a hanging loop. Working from the top down, she applies a dab of hot glue to a paint‑chip circle, places the yarn between two circles, and presses them together before the glue sets; she repeats this, adding four to six circles at a time, mixing colors randomly to avoid patterns. After the glue dries, each completed strand—some entirely painted, others plain yarn alternating—is ready. The strands are then hung side‑by‑side in front of the window, where daylight and later evening light illuminate the colorful “beads.” The presenter thanks viewers, invites them to try the project, and the video ends with the usual end‑screen and channel‑promotion graphics.
